/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.headline: Far-right and Iran add to mix of terror threats UK faces – not to mention AI
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.excerpt: MI5’s annual threat update covers so much ground it is easy to feel anxious. The terror threat has become more diverse, with far-right anti-migrant threats on the rise; while Iran has now firmly emerged alongside Russia as a country seeking to undertake violent and deadly plots in the UK. “There is no law of physics dictating that rising state threats will be accompanied by diminishing terrorist threats,” MI5’s director general, Ken McCallum, said, although one of his core messages was that people and the country at large needed to focus on being more resilient. “In this new world, we should expect to be tested.” A key issue highlighted by McCallum was that years of anti-migrant, anti-Muslim hostility had now led to an increase in cases where people were “tipping into terrorist intent” – that is crossing the line from rhetoric to violence. It is a complex area, but one certainly fuelled by political hate narratives and online subcultures. It is also fuelled by toxic rhetoric from abroad. Authoritarian regimes, McCallum said, were investing heavily “in trying to distort and divide our society” – although he was too polite to mention that there is plenty of evidence that voices from the US led by X owner Elon Musk are keen to sow division in the UK too, as they post about flashpoint events such as the June rioting in Belfast and Southampton.
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.trail: Annual update from MI5 chief highlighted a complex cocktail that could have real-life consequences for Britain

/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.headline: Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.excerpt: Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum through social media and television reports, the head of MI5 said on Tuesday, but he added that did not mean the Kremlin had any impact on the result. Ken McCallum endorsed comments by Andy Burnham, who raised the issue over the past two days, though he said continuing to debate it risked giving the Kremlin a needless propaganda victory. During an annual threat update, the head of Britain’s domestic intelligence agency said the Russian-owned English-language broadcasters RT and Sputnik “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” with biased anti-migration and anti-EU reports. He said there had also been “a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”: an unspecified number of fake social media accounts, operating largely on X, that had sought to influence the result. Neither tactic was particularly sophisticated or successful, the spy chief said. There was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”. Both interference attempts have been previously cited in studies released in the years after the Brexit vote. The digital campaign group 89up said RT and Sputnik had published 261 mostly misleading articles highlighting immigration and other anti-EU issues that achieved 134m potential page impressions.
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.trail: Ken McCallum says Kremlin attempted to influence vote through social media and TV reports but had little impact

/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.headline: MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.excerpt: The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival. The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”. The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency. China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work. This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers. Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert, warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.trail: Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting

/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.headline: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.excerpt: MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects. Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023. The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service. On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side. “Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations.
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.trail: Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence

/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.headline: Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.excerpt: British intelligence has been given assurances by its Israeli counterpart that information sharing with the UK will continue as before, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has said. The disclosure counters predictions that his decision to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements would lead to a collapse in cooperation between the agencies. The exchanges of information are seen as mutually beneficial and it is understood that Israeli intelligence was never willing to become mired in any political dispute between the two governments. Miliband insists the intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband also expressed confidence that the US shared some of his exasperation with Israel’s reluctance to constrain the settlers in the West Bank, or to engage fully with the 20-point plan for Gaza set out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. As yet there has been no explicit criticism of the UK’s actions by the White House. Trump avoided taking a hard stance when pressed about the coalition of countries, including the UK, France, and Canada, that have imposed new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. “I’ll be speaking to Israel, I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what’s their thinking,” he said on Wednesday.
/uk-news/2026/oct/13/rightwing-extremist.trail: UK foreign secretary says international community including US shares ‘frustration’ at Israel’s failure to constrain illegal settlers

/world/2026/oct/13/pope-leo-hospital-ope.headline: Man of his word: Pope Leo speeches declared human-authored by Australian AI detection tool
/world/2026/oct/13/pope-leo-hospital-ope.excerpt: A collection of speeches and writings by Pope Leo XIV has been certified as human-authored less than two months after Leo declared artificial intelligence the greatest threat to humanity. Proudly Human, the Australian company spearheaded by Australia’s former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel, undertook a review of a collection of writings and speeches by the pope, in collaboration with the publisher, the Australian Catholic University and cardinals in the Vatican. Maps of Hope was published in the same week in May that Leo’s first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, warned of the dangers of artificial intelligence and the risks of the power of the technology being concentrated in the hands of a few. In the encyclical, Leo said AI should be prevented “from dominating humanity,” adding that the technology should be “human-friendly”, accessible to all and open to discussion and debate. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Finkel told Guardian Australia he had a “great deal of confidence” going into the Maps of Hope process that Leo’s speeches would be human-written by a human, and within a day, Proudly Human had certified the collection as human-created. The process typically requires authors or their representatives to sign up to the site, go through an ID check, and sign a declaration that they are operating within minimum standards: AI can’t be used to write the first draft, or write sentences and paragraphs.
/world/2026/oct/13/pope-leo-hospital-ope.trail: Maps of Hope has been certified by Proudly Human, a company led by former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel

/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.headline: Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says minister
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.excerpt: An AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister. Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity. In a speech Narayan said an incident in June when an OpenAI agent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK. “It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.” Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that it was not authorised to have. “The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said. Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI. The government will also consider using the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.trail: Kanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by artificial intelligence agent

/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.headline: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.excerpt: OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI. The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September. However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported. Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment. OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn. News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%. The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July. Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not.
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.trail: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before

/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.headline: Anthropic bans users from ‘needless abusive or cruel behavior’ towards Claude
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.excerpt: Anthropic has barred users from exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness. The Verge first reported the change in policy. A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is behind the AI chatbot Claude, did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what could be considered “abusive or cruel”. In an online user policy, the San Francisco-based company noted that its ban would not apply to common user frustrations, model testing or “dark creative themes”. Anthropic’s usage policy previously contained restrictions on abusive conduct. The company’s large language models have the ability to end a conversation if a user is being persistently harmful. When that feature rolled out last August, the company framed it as a safeguard for AI’s welfare. “We remain highly uncertain about the potential moral status of Claude and other LLMs, now or in the future. However, we take the issue seriously, and alongside our research program we’re working to identify and implement low-cost interventions to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case such welfare is possible. Allowing models to end or exit potentially distressing interactions is one such intervention,” according to its website. The notion of AI systems being conscious has been highly polarizing in and outside the tech world. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has said he cannot rule out the possibility.
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.trail: A spokesperson for the tech company did not specify what kind of behavior would be considered abusive

/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.headline: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.excerpt: Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology. The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”. In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down after one of its researchers quit, warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. “I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely]. “I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.trail: Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver

/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.headline: Rural Queenslanders have seen gas projects come and go – but a 725-hectare datacentre poses a whole new level of ‘stupidity’
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.excerpt: From the veranda on his bush block, Denver Kanowski has watched resources companies come and go from rural Queensland for 70 years. The home cost him $800, and lets him live how he likes, in nature. It’s also in the middle of a gasfield, not far from the Linc Energy contamination site, down the road from a coalmine and three gas power plants. Last month came the biggest scheme yet, a $31bn datacentre to power Claude, the large language model developed by global AI giant Anthropic. If built, Australia’s largest datacentre would be about 15 minutes’ drive away from Kanowski’s home, outside Kogan, near Dalby, about 180km west of Brisbane. In a community that has seen the boom and bust of coal seam gas, the response from many has been the same as Kanowski’s: once bitten, twice shy. “This is the power of money and the power of greed and shortsighted stupidity,” Kanowski says. “I’ve read this book before.” Anthropic’s project is to be built on a 725-hectare plot of land now occupied by a 24,000-head feedlot, surrounded by gas wells. According to Singapore-based developer Zerra DC, its cooling system will be far less water intensive than that used in most existing datacentres, generating about the same demand as an average shopping centre. But like all AI, it will require an enormous amount of energy. The Western Downs datacentre will require a peak power capacity equal to about a quarter of total state energy demand, 2.16GW.
/technology/2026/oct/13/anthropic-ai-rep.trail: Residents of Dalby may soon live beside a $31bn datacentre. The premier sees ‘opportunity’ for the state – but others fear AI’s global creep

/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.headline: BBC seeks to subpoena Trump children and son-in-law over defamation lawsuit
/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.excerpt: The BBC is trying to subpoena Donald Trump’s children as it builds its defense against the president’s defamation lawsuit centered on a documentary on the January 6 insurrection. In a motion filed on Friday, the BBC sought authorization to serve Trump’s two eldest children, Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump, and son-in-law Jared Kushner, with subpoenas for testimony and their records on the events of 6 January 2021. The BBC, its lawyers wrote in court documents, is entitled to discover Trump’s “intention behind the speech and anything that bears on the impression his audience could have reasonably obtained in listening to the speech”, which includes whether Trump “gave it intentionally or otherwise; the breadth of the audience of the message and impression; and the extent of any resulting injury or harm”. Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in December over scenes in the 2024 BBC documentary Trump, A Second Chance?. It argued that the BBC spliced scenes from Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech so that it appeared Trump directly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol building. Trump’s children and son-in-law have, “without question”, knowledge of several incidents that day, BBC’s lawyers wrote, , including when Trump sought to convince former vice-president Mike Pence to refuse certifying the results of the 2020 election. The BBC also said that Kushner allegedly helped to draft a statement for Trump that would have condemned the use of violence at the Capitol.
/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.trail: Network wants to serve Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr after president sues over January 6 documentary

/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.headline: US federal judge halts order for Trump to turn over financial records to BBC
/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.excerpt: A federal judge has temporarily halted an order requiring Donald Trump to turn over detailed financial information about his business empire to the BBC as part of an ongoing libel lawsuit. US district judge Roy Altman issued the temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise and narrow parts of his lawsuit against the BBC over a 2024 documentary that aired in the UK. Trump’s legal team sought to stop the discovery order that would have given the BBC access to the president’s financial records in the multibillion-dollar case. Trump has argued the BBC’s 2024 documentary about the January 6 attack harmed his business interests. Last month, a Miami-based judge ruled that Trump would have to begin producing extensive financial records by 6 August, including information covering the hundreds of businesses held by the Trump family trust. On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys asked the court to temporarily suspend that order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”. In a four-page order signed on Wednesday and released on Thursday, Altman said Trump’s effort to remove his claims that the documentary damaged his brand and businesses could reduce the BBC’s need to obtain his financial records. Trump’s lawyers are seeking to narrow the claim to alleged reputational harm.
/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.trail: Judge issues temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise his libel lawsuit against BBC

/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.headline: Trump team pushes to block court order giving BBC access to financial records
/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.excerpt: Donald Trump’s legal team is making an 11th-hour attempt to block a court order that would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster. Trump claims that the BBC’s 2024 documentary on the January 6 attacks have damaged the president’s business interests. In July, a Miami-based judge ruled that the president would have to start handing over detailed financial records to the BBC by 6 August. The records would reveal details into the hundreds of businesses owned by the US president’s family trust. Trump’s attorneys asked the court on Wednesday to temporarily pause the enforcement of the court order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”. Trump’s lawyers also asked the court to amend their initial lawsuit to instead focus on the “reputation harm” that was caused by the documentary, which would keep necessary disclosures “proportional to the needs of the case”, the lawyers said. While it is unclear what Trump’s net worth is, recent financial disclosures showed that he had made more than $2.2bn during his first year back in office. The lawsuit against the BBC is one of Trump’s several recent attempts to wage legal battles against media outlets that publish critical coverage of him.
/media/2026/oct/13/bbc-trump-lawsuit-dep.trail: President has sued the broadcaster for $10bn, claiming a documentary on 2021 Capitol attack led to financial harm

/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.headline: Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.excerpt: Andy Burnham has promised a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s future place in Europe, saying the existing relationship is “not good enough” as he framed next month’s Brussels summit as a possible first step to EU membership. The prime minister said Britain must take a “clear-eyed rational look” at its long-term relationship with the bloc to boost economic growth and control immigration, which needed to go beyond Labour’s existing red lines. The next “reset” summit will take place on 20 November, ending months of uncertainty, with the two sides seeking to sign deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading, which Burnham hopes could provide a £10bn-a-year boost to the economy. One EU diplomat said a deal on the three “significant but modest” issues needed to be approved as a test of the UK’s good faith so both sides could get on with the “real reset” in the longer-term relationship. But the UK remains braced for a possible row over protectionist “Made in Europe” trade rules amid industry fears they could lock out UK manufacturers, prompting the prime minister to pledge he would raise concerns with his EU counterparts. Burnham was also forced to clarify that he did not think Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit campaign had affected the final result, after he raised questions about the legitimacy of the outcome in comments at the weekend.
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.trail: PM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematic

/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.headline: Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.excerpt: Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street. Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had. Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.” Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote. The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote. A report by parliament’s intelligence and security committee in 2020 criticised the government and intelligence agencies for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum. The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts.
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.trail: PM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddled

/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.headline: Ball in UK’s court: EU ambassador says Brussels will be ‘ready to engage‘ after country decides what it wants
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.excerpt: Jukka Salovaara, the newly installed European Union ambassador to the UK, is likely to become a ubiquitous figure in national politics as the Andy Burnham government grapples with the question of its future relationship with the European Union. Burnham has been clearer than his predecessor Keir Starmer in saying that what exists now is not working and that a full range of options, including rejoining, has to be on the table ahead of Labour’s next election manifesto. Salovaara, aged 58, sees his role over the coming years as a “facilitator”, testing both sides like a good diplomat on what might fly and what will not work. He will not sit at the negotiating table, but he will be “very close to it”. “Everyone tells me my job is explaining London to Brussels and Brussels to London”. The UK, he says, remains “the European Union’s first and foremost partner”. When the two have made agreements, it has always been to “our mutual benefit”. A former permanent secretary in Finland’s foreign ministry, who also served as his country’s ambassador to the UN, this is his first job with the European Commission, but not his first posting in the UK. As a young diplomat in the summer of 1996, he handled European affairs in London for Finland at the onset of Cool Britannia, just as Tony Blair was on the cusp of gaining power. “The 1990s was such an optimistic time,” he says of that era. “World trade was growing.
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.trail: Jukka Salovaara, who served in London during Cool Britannia era, will be ‘very close’ to negotiations as Burnham government resets relations with EU

/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.headline: Half of UK wants to rejoin EU and backing it could drive up Labour vote, megapoll finds
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.excerpt: Andy Burnham’s personal preference to rejoin the European Union after the next election is supported by almost half of all voters, a new megapoll has found, although cabinet ministers concerned about reopening Brexit divides are privately urging him to proceed with caution. The poll by the Messina Group (TMG) found that renegotiating the UK’s relationship with the EU could boost Labour’s vote share by as much as seven points, if the prime minister offered a fresh referendum in which he campaigned to re-enter the bloc. Almost a third of voters said an in-out referendum would be needed first, while more than one in six felt that a general election mandate would be sufficient, and the same proportion thought parliament could make the decision. The overall findings will bolster the case of those inside Downing Street who want to promise at the next election that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry, which the prime minister has said he wants to see “in his lifetime”. Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as leader on Tuesday to announce a review of the options for Britain’s future relationship with Europe, and subsequently added that these should include rejoining entirely. However, there are nerves among some Labour MPs, especially those with constituencies that voted for Brexit, that even testing out public support for the move would be fraught with political risk and a potential boost to Reform.
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.trail: Exclusive: Findings will bolster those in No 10 who want to negotiate on re-entry but some senior figures remain wary

/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.headline: Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.excerpt: Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said. Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro. “Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.” Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.
/politics/2026/oct/13/burnham-to-host-ze.trail: Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’

/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.headline: David Ellison denies he has ‘politicized’ Skydance despite close Trump links
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.excerpt: David Ellison, the chief executive of the newly formed media conglomerate Skydance, denied that he had “politicized” the company despite the close connection he has forged with Donald Trump’s White House over the 20 months of his administration. “We have a good relationship with this administration,” Ellison acknowledged to reporters at a Tuesday press briefing focused on the now-consummated merger of Paramount Skydance and CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery. “I also had a really good relationship with President Biden. I have a good relationship with [Republican South Carolina senator] Tim Scott, and I have a good relationship with Governor Gavin Newsom. I think it is important to talk to everybody on both sides of the aisle … When you’re operating within a business-friendly administration, you should always have those relationships. “We want to speak to everybody,” Ellison added. “We do not want to politicize the company.” Asked about his conversations with Trump about CNN, Ellison did not directly discuss his communications with the president, the network’s most prominent critic. But he said he wanted to clarify that “we have not talked to any political leader of any party about news, other than to say that we want to be in the truth business and we want to be in the trust business.

/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.headline: White House removes CNN from press pool for second time in a week
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.excerpt: For a second time in a week, the White House has unilaterally removed CNN from its assignment as the primary television pool representative covering Donald Trump. CNN was excluded on Saturday from pool duty onboard Air Force One, despite a district judge’s ruling – two days earlier – overturning the White House’s ban on the network and two other media organizations. But on Sunday, in what appeared to be a thawing of tensions, the White House published a pool assignment list that listed CNN as in-town pooler for Thursday’s activities, with the conservative network Real America’s Voice serving as secondary pooler. Then, on Wednesday night, the White House abruptly removed CNN from pool duty for the following day, leaving Real America’s Voice as the only pooler as the president travels to Texas and Oklahoma. The country’s largest broadcast and cable television news networks have not aired Real America’s Voice footage, though the network has widely broadcast its availability. The five networks that serve in the primary television pool have taken it day by day since the White House originally banned CNN on 18 September, initially suspending operation before tentatively kicking back into action this past Friday. As they did on Saturday, none of the other four networks will take CNN’s place on Thursday, meaning there will be no primary pool footage, though networks could cover individual parts of his trip. CNN did not comment on the network’s exclusion on Thursday.

/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.headline: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.excerpt: Donald Trump’s attorney general, Todd Blanche, argued on Sunday that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting. Blanche offered no evidence for his claim that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate, rather than simply unflattering to the president. Pressed by the interviewer, Martha Raddatz, to point to a report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate. “Wait, give you an example of when CNN doesn’t report accurately? You cannot be asking me that,” Blanche replied. “There’s not even a real dispute that the information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100% negative toward the president.” On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.trail: US attorney general argues that president was ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico

/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.headline: Trump tells female MS Now reporter to be ‘quiet’ amid questions on press pool ban
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.excerpt: A day after the White House barred CNN from traveling onboard Air Force One to provide pool television coverage of the president’s trip to Tennessee, Donald Trump doubled down on his criticism of that broadcaster and another, MS Now, he has attempted to ban over coverage of him he calls overly negative. As he left the White House early on Saturday, Trump was asked by the MS Now White House correspondent Akayla Gardner: “Do you only want outlets that support you to be a part of the press pool?” “No, no, no. I want real news, not fake news – like you,” Trump replied, in a moment that was not broadcast live, due to the removal of CNN as the designated pool television crew, but was posted on social media by the White House. As Trump continued on, repeating past insults about CNN and MS Now, which he called “MS DNC”, in reference to the Democratic National Committee, Gardner pressed him harder: “Do you not want tough questions?” “Quiet,” Trump said, before continuing to air his familiar grievance that their reporting on him is not flattering enough. Since his first presidency, Trump has labeled non-partisan news outlets that do not openly support him “the enemy of the people”, maligning unfavorable reports as “fake news”. In his second term, he has increasingly told female reporters who ask him challenging questions to be quiet.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.trail: US president doubles down on criticism of CNN and MS Now as Akayla Gardner questions attempted White House ban

/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.headline: White House blocks CNN from Air Force One in latest escalation with news media
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.excerpt: The White House has blocked CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One on Saturday, impeding its TV press pool duties in the latest escalation of the administration’s battle with the news media. CNN had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, the network said on Friday. The White House confirmed CNN’s exclusion when it did not list the network on guidance sent to the press corps regarding Trump’s schedule for Saturday. CNN’s exclusion from Air Force One was first reported by the Washington Post. The White House did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment. The incident comes a week after Trump, a vocal critic of what he deems the “fake news media”, revoked White House access for CNN, Politico, and MS Now, citing unfavorable reports about his presidency. The Republican president published a post about the topic on his Truth Social platform early on Saturday which read: “Why should perpetrators of FAKE NEWS … be allowed access to a very sacred place, the White House? Despite my big Election Win, almost 100% of ‘TRUMP’ coverage is negative, and has been for years!” The post singled out CNN and MS Now, referring to the latter as MSDNC, which combined the outlet’s name with the Democratic National Committee. He published it days after a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/white-house-media-b.trail: Outlet had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, network said Friday

/global-development/2026/oct/14/najmeh-a.headline: Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for help
/global-development/2026/oct/14/najmeh-a.excerpt: The family of 21-year-old twins who have been sentenced respectively to death and decades in jail for protesting against the Iranian regime have appealed to the United Nations for help. A formal “submission of information” relating to the case of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi has been submitted by British human right lawyers on their family’s behalf. The move could lead to the UN’s human rights council opening talks with the Iranian regime about resolving the case if it is found to involve human rights violations. The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, told the UN’s general assembly in New York this week that the country was “ready for dialogue and diplomacy”. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps eight months ago after they joined nationwide protests against the regime. They were tried over charges that included moharebeh (waging war against God) for taking to the streets of Isfahan, in central Iran, on 8 and 9 January. At the end of August, Taraneh, along with nine others, was sentenced to death. Romina received a 25-year prison sentence. The girls’ family are seeking to appeal against the sentences but human rights groups have raised concerns that Taraneh’s execution could be fast-tracked. The women are being held in Dowlatabad prison in Isfahan, where the twins’ family claim that Taraneh was threatened with being forced to watch the rape of her sister if she failed to sign a confession to her alleged crimes.
/global-development/2026/oct/14/najmeh-a.trail: Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regime

/science/2026/oct/14/focus-on-sounds-to-.headline: Açaí, chipotle and gnocchi – and other words you are probably mispronouncing
/science/2026/oct/14/focus-on-sounds-to-.excerpt: Name: Açaí. Age: First imported to western countries from South America as freeze-dried pulp in the 1990s. Appearance: A small, dark-purple berry, or a purée made from them, commonly used in smoothies. It has bits coming off it. Sorry? There’s a sort of chin whisker hanging from the “c” and something weird is going on with the dot over the “i”. Those are accents, designed to help you pronounce the word correctly. They’re no help to me. That could explain why açaí is the most mispronounced word in the UK, often rendered in speech as “ack-eye” or “ah-sigh”. How should I be saying it? “Ah-sigh-ee”. Seriously? Açaí is just the tip of the iceberg. It tops a new list of 20 commonly mispronounced words. What are some others? Quinoa came fourth; gnocchi came fifth; chipotle was seventh. Are you sure this isn’t a list of Britain’s least-ordered menu items? Not all the words on the list are foods. Segue, often mispronounced “seeg” instead of “segway”, was second. Worcestershire came sixth. What? Knowing how to pronounce Worcestershire is the only advantage Britons have over the rest of the world. Those days are over. Who came up with this list? It’s from a recent poll of 2,000 people commissioned by Škoda. Why would a Czech car company care how I pronounce chipotle? I think it is trying to make a point because Škoda is often mispronounced as “scoder” rather than “shkoda”. And, obviously, it’s a publicity thing. Does Škoda think it’s good publicity to humiliate a country?
/science/2026/oct/14/focus-on-sounds-to-.trail: The English language can seem designed to trip us up, whether we’re greeting a colonel or travelling to Worcestershire. Here are some of the biggest stumbling blocks
